attempts.raw_response: She unbolted them cautiously and peered out. Below her lay a small courtyard, cluttered with empty barrels and packing-cases. A wall bordered it on the far side, and beyond the wall she could see the open road. To climb down seemed perilous, yet far less dreadful than remaining where she was. She listened intently. The voices of the men were still audible, but fainter now, as though they had moved toward the front of the building. Summoning all her courage, she swung the doors wide, gripped the sill, and lowered herself over the edge, her feet searching for some foothold among the crates below. Her fingers burned against the rough wood. She held her breath and let go, dropping softly onto a barrel, which rocked beneath her weight but did not overturn.

pair.human_continuation:
The iron hook yielded readily to her grasp, and one door stuck
fast, while the other opened a few inches. She looked out upon a green
<DW72> covered with flowers and bunches of sage and bushes. Neither man
nor horse showed in the narrow field of her vision. She believed she
would be safer hidden out there in the shrubbery than in the house. The
jump from the window would be easy for her. And with her quick decision
came a rush and stir of spirit that warded off her weakness.

She pulled at the door. It did not budge. It had caught at the bottom.
Pulling with all her might proved to be in vain.
pair.prefix:
Madeline lost faith in her hiding-place. Moreover, she found it
impossible to take the chance. The idea of being caught in that dark
room by those ruffians filled her with horror. She must get out into the
light. Swiftly she rose and went to the window. It was rather more of a
door than window, being a large aperture closed by two wooden doors on
hinges.

source_document.title: The Light of Western Stars by Zane Grey
